title: Fault-tolerant quantum computer with useful, scalable logical computation

concept.text: A useful, scalable fault-tolerant quantum computer would preserve quantum information while carrying out a complete, programmable calculation. It would encode logical qubits across physical qubits, detect and manage errors, and perform logical operations without allowing errors to accumulate beyond the calculation’s success target. The innovation is the integrated capability: physical hardware, control, error correction, decoding and logical gates working reliably together throughout a long algorithm.

Protecting a stored quantum state, demonstrating a universal set of logical gates and executing a small encoded algorithm are important milestones with different scopes. Memory protection tests whether information survives storage. A universal logical toolbox supplies operations sufficient in principle to express arbitrary quantum computations. The proposed innovation additionally requires those operations to remain reliable as complete computations grow, with tolerable physical resources, runtime and discarded-run costs. The supplied demonstrations establish parts of that capability rather than its useful, scalable completion.

significance.text: Sustained error suppression during logical operations would allow quantum algorithms to run deeper and more reliably than hardware whose errors accumulate unchecked. A consequential, independently verified advantage over credible classical alternatives would establish a useful computational capability for the demonstrated workload. This would be revolutionary because it would connect quantum information processing’s theoretical possibilities to dependable computation under an explicit performance and resource budget. That impact remains conditional on successful integration and a convincing application demonstration.

Conditional application possibilities include molecular simulation, materials research and cryptanalysis. Their feasibility would depend on the algorithm, problem instance, required accuracy and available logical resources; the supplied papers do not establish application-specific feasibility in these areas. Useful quantum advantage on one workload would not imply faster computation for every problem, nor would a universal gate set guarantee practical advantage. This is an impact synthesis, not a forecast or a demonstrated application result.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is sustained, scalable error control during complete logical computations. Errors must be removed while encoded information is manipulated, and the combined process must improve the probability of completing the whole algorithm successfully. A low error rate during storage or a short gate sequence does not by itself establish this. The neutral-atom paper explicitly identifies deep-circuit testing and optimization as remaining work, while the trapped-ion paper leaves higher-distance performance thresholds and overheads for future investigation.

Concrete engineering barriers include coordinating qubit operations, error extraction, decoding and subsequent control within the machine’s timing constraints. The neutral-atom work discusses control, cooling, decoder scalability and clock speed as coupled constraints. Increasing protection must produce enough reliability improvement to justify the additional operations and resources. Several demonstrated logical operations used software feedforward, so their results alone do not establish a complete real-time control loop operating at the scale and speed required by long algorithms.

Postselection introduces another integration challenge: an experiment can reject runs in which final checks detect errors, improving the quality of retained outputs while reducing the chance of obtaining a usable result per attempt. Both supplied papers use postselection in relevant demonstrations. Scalable computation therefore requires accounting for accepted-run accuracy, acceptance probability, retries and total runtime together. In particular, a measurement-free logical gate protocol with final error detection does not by itself establish sustained, scalable error correction throughout an arbitrary long computation.

current_state.text: Bluvstein and colleagues’ “A fault-tolerant neutral-atom architecture for universal quantum computation,” published online on 10 November 2025, reports experiments using a logical processor with up to 448 atoms. The work demonstrates key architectural components, including repeated error correction and logical operations. The atom count describes the physical experimental scale; it is not a count of 448 logical qubits.

The neutral-atom below-threshold benchmark used four rounds of correction. Several logical-operation demonstrations used postselection and software feedforward. These are meaningful component demonstrations, but the finite correction sequence and experimental qualifications limit what can be inferred about long, fully integrated calculations. The paper identifies remaining scalability constraints and calls for testing and optimization in deep circuits; it does not demonstrate the proposed useful, large-scale end-to-end advantage.

Butt and colleagues’ 2026 paper, “Demonstration of measurement-free universal logical quantum computation,” reports a trapped-ion fault-tolerant universal logical toolbox and a small Grover search on three logical qubits encoded in an eight-qubit error-detecting code. The protocols use final error detection and postselection. The measurement-free description concerns the logical protocols and should not be read as eliminating final checks or demonstrating continuous scalable correction.

The experimental logical Grover search achieved an overall single-shot solution probability of 0.40(4), below the paper’s optimal classical comparison of 0.46. Thus, this experiment demonstrates encoded algorithm execution without outperforming that comparison. Proposed improvements discussed through simulations are prospective results, not measured experimental improvements. The result neither establishes useful quantum advantage nor invalidates the value of the demonstrated logical operations.

The supplied review assessed an extraction of the neutral-atom article that ends mid-sentence on page 17. Relevant earlier passages were available, but the review does not establish independent inspection of figure images or omitted supplementary material. The trapped-ion article’s supplied extraction covers the complete 12-page article; separate supplements were not supplied. These access boundaries limit the evidence assessed without implying that either reported result is false.

The supplied materials also mention an earlier Google below-threshold surface-code memory result, but provide no independently assessed source for its details. It therefore remains background context rather than an additional verified demonstration in this record. More broadly, the empty freshness record means that these dated papers do not establish an exhaustive account of the field as of 1 November 2026. They support the milestones described here without settling whether later work has advanced the integrated capability.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: operate a programmable universal logical processor through a substantial end-to-end algorithm with repeated error correction. Define the algorithm, workload, output accuracy, success target and resource budget in advance so that “substantial” and “useful” have assessable meanings. Include all preparation, logical operations, correction, control decisions and final readout needed to produce the result. These are proposed evaluation criteria, not established standards.
completion_criteria.label: Universal logical processor completes substantial computation with repeated error correction

completion_criteria.text: Proposed scaling test: increase protection and show that total algorithm failure decreases under otherwise comparable conditions. Report both the accuracy of accepted outputs and the probability of obtaining an accepted output, including rejected runs and retry costs. Exercise multiple circuit depths and operation patterns to distinguish storage performance from performance during computation. Such finite tests would establish the processor’s demonstrated breadth and scaling behavior, not literal reliability for every possible computation.
completion_criteria.label: Total algorithm failure decreases with increased protection during computation

completion_criteria.text: Proposed usefulness test: solve a specified consequential problem with a transparent advantage over credible classical alternatives at comparable accuracy and confidence. State whether the claimed advantage concerns runtime, cost, energy or another practical measure. Include auxiliary qubits, decoding, classical control, cooling, runtime, postselection and verification costs in the resource accounting. A convincing result should remain meaningful within an explicitly stated operating envelope rather than depend on unreported exclusions.
completion_criteria.label: Consequential problem shows practical advantage with full resource accounting

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility requirement: disclose enough hardware conditions, logical protocols, decoding methods, acceptance rules and outcome data for independent assessment and reproduction. Replication should test both the reliability trend and the claimed practical advantage, with uncertainties and unsuccessful runs included. Document the supported problem sizes, operating conditions and failure boundaries so that a successful demonstration does not become an unsupported claim of universal practical superiority.
completion_criteria.label: Methods and outcomes enable independent replication within documented limits

related_concepts.text: Roster comparison synthesis: ELE-03, “A long-distance quantum repeater network,” overlaps through quantum information storage, error management and reliable operations. Its central outcome is transmitting quantum information or entanglement across distance, whereas ELE-02 concerns reliable algorithm execution. Advances may share enabling techniques, but neither completion criterion establishes the other.

Roster comparison synthesis: ELE-04, “Practical, energy-recovering reversible computing,” overlaps with quantum computation’s use of reversible operations. Its defining objective is practical energy recovery in computation. ELE-02 instead requires preserving encoded quantum information through useful logical calculations; it does not by itself establish low total energy consumption or energy-recovering hardware.

Roster comparison synthesis: ELE-11, “Integrated photonic-electronic computing with broad system advantage,” shares the need to demonstrate benefits after accounting for complete system overhead. Photonic and electronic components could contribute to quantum hardware or control, but ELE-11’s title does not require fault-tolerant quantum computation. The two entries concern distinct computational capabilities.

Roster comparison synthesis: ELE-01, “Practical ambient-temperature superconducting conductors,” and ELE-08, “Manufacturable ultra-low-voltage switching for general-purpose electronics,” could affect supporting hardware, power or control costs in some implementations. Neither capability is established here as a prerequisite for ELE-02, and neither would itself solve quantum error correction or logical-computation scaling.

Roster comparison synthesis: ELE-05, “Cheap, scalable storage for weeks to seasons of electrical supply”; ELE-07, “Infrastructure-scale wireless electrical power delivery”; and ELE-09, “Resilient, self-restoring power networks,” address electrical infrastructure rather than encoded computation. ELE-06, “Durable, high-bandwidth two-way neural interface,” and ELE-10, “Broadly deployable, maintenance-free ambient-powered sensing,” address distinct interface and sensing capabilities. Their broad connection through electronics does not establish a specific technical dependency or justify merging them with ELE-02.

unresolved_issues: The supplied freshness record is empty; whether additional work changes the field’s status as of 1 November 2026 remains unresolved.
The Google below-threshold surface-code memory result and earlier citation history cannot be independently assessed from the supplied artifacts.

The neutral-atom extraction is truncated on page 17, and independent inspection of figure images and omitted supplementary material is not established. Separate supplements for the trapped-ion article were not supplied.
A concrete completion assessment still needs a selected workload, accuracy and success targets, resource budget, classical comparison and reproducibility protocol.
Application-specific feasibility for molecular simulation, materials research and cryptanalysis is not established by the supplied papers.
The supplied demonstrations do not settle how total algorithm reliability, acceptance probability and full system overhead will scale in long integrated computations.

brief.title: Reliable quantum computers for useful calculations
possible: Researchers could run long quantum calculations while the machine continually corrects errors. Quantum bits, the units that hold quantum information, would work together to protect information throughout a calculation. Increasing that protection would let the machine reliably complete larger tasks.
why: This would let researchers carry out calculations that errors currently prevent them from completing reliably. Potential uses include simulating molecules, studying materials and breaking encryption. A practical advantage on an important problem would give people a new computational tool.

sources.showed: Using uncharged atoms, they demonstrated repeated error correction and operations on protected quantum bits. A benchmark showed that stronger protection reduced errors over four correction rounds.
sources.quote:
On injecting global coherent 
errors at regular intervals, we find repeated correction significantly 
suppresses logical errors
sources.cited_for: The work demonstrates components needed to protect quantum information while computing.
sources.not_established: Long, complete calculations still need to demonstrate reliable operation and a practical advantage, including the cost of discarded attempts.

sources.showed: Using trapped ions, electrically charged atoms, they demonstrated operations sufficient to express arbitrary quantum calculations. They also ran a small quantum search using protected quantum bits.
sources.quote:
In this work, we
propose and experimentally demonstrate a universal toolbox of fault-tolerant
logical operations on error-detecting codes without mid-circuit measurements
on a trapped-ion quantum processor.
sources.cited_for: The work demonstrates a complete set of protected operations and their use in a small algorithm.
sources.not_established: The search performed below its classical comparison, and final error checks discarded runs. Sustained correction during long calculations remains.

shown: Bluvstein and colleagues demonstrated repeated correction alongside building blocks for programmable quantum computing. Butt and colleagues used protected quantum bits to execute a small search algorithm. Together, these experiments demonstrate error control, computing operations and encoded algorithm execution.
missing: A substantial, complete calculation must succeed with repeated error correction throughout preparation, operations and final readout.
Stronger protection must improve whole-calculation success while accounting for discarded runs, retries and total runtime.
A consequential problem must show a practical advantage over credible classical methods, with all supporting resources counted.
Independent teams must reproduce both the reliability improvement and the practical advantage.

milestones.label: A substantial calculation succeeds with repeated error correction
milestones.explanation: A programmable processor would have to complete a substantial algorithm with repeated correction and predefined accuracy, success and resource targets. This would demonstrate that the components work together throughout a calculation.

milestones.label: Stronger protection reduces total calculation failure
milestones.explanation: Increasing protection would have to reduce total failure across varied calculation lengths and operations, counting rejected runs and retries. This would establish whether reliability improves as protection grows.

milestones.label: An important problem gains a practical advantage
milestones.explanation: A consequential problem would have to beat credible classical alternatives at comparable accuracy, counting all resources and verification costs. This would establish usefulness within stated operating conditions.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce reliability and practical advantage
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce the reliability trend and practical advantage using disclosed methods and outcomes, including failures. This would establish reproducibility and the limits of the demonstrated capability.

uncertain: How will total reliability, discarded-run rates and supporting resource needs change as complete calculations grow longer?
Which workload, accuracy target, resource budget and classical comparison should define a convincing demonstration?

page.title: Utility-scale fault-tolerant quantum computing
page.definition: A programmable quantum computer protects logical qubits—quantum bits encoded across physical components—by correcting errors throughout computation. It delivers computation whose monetary value exceeds its cost, DARPA’s definition of utility-scale operation.

goal.need: Google’s below-threshold study contrasts 99.9% physical entangling-gate fidelity with error requirements below 10^-10 for many applications. DOE distinguishes a prototype running a scientific subroutine from a fault-tolerant computer executing a complete scientific workflow.

figures.caption: DOE’s illustrative prototype and scientific-workflow benchmarks.
figures.note: Hard operations are gates needed for universality that are costly in the chosen code. DOE negotiates acceptance metrics.

statements.quote: develop and deploy scientifically relevant, fault-tolerant quantum computing capabilities for research and development.
statements.context: The stated purpose of Quantum Genesis.

statements.quote: a large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computer capable of running quantum circuits comprising 100 million quantum gates on 200 logical qubits.
statements.context: The published capability target for IBM Quantum Starling.

statements.quote: whether any quantum computing approach can achieve utility-scale operation
statements.context: The question the Quantum Benchmarking Initiative seeks to verify and validate.

completion.title: A fault-tolerant quantum computer delivers computation whose value exceeds its cost.
completion.criterion: An operating, programmable fault-tolerant quantum computer achieves DARPA QBI’s utility-scale condition: computational value exceeds cost. QBI’s Q&A discusses value in dollars and asks developers to justify its quantification. Its public definition does not fix a workload, qubit count, operation count or common cost model. Passing QBI’s component-and-prototype validation stage alone does not establish utility-scale operation.
completion.set_by: DARPA, Quantum Benchmarking Initiative programme definition and accompanying Q&A.
completion.threshold_quote: utility-scale operation — meaning its computational value exceeds its cost.
completion.basis: DARPA’s published condition addresses the usefulness and cost of the integrated computer. Its Q&A explicitly discusses fault-tolerant, gate-based systems. DOE’s scientific-workflow milestone permits classically tractable demonstrations, so passing that milestone does not establish the economic condition.

milestones.title: A corrected logical qubit stores information longer than its best physical component.
milestones.criterion: An actively corrected logical qubit retains quantum coherence longer than every constituent quantum component used in its correction process. Sivak and colleagues, published on 22 March 2023, demonstrated one oscillator-encoded logical qubit with a coherence-lifetime gain of 2.27 ± 0.07 over the best constituent component.
milestones.set_by: The quantum-error-correction community’s break-even convention, applied by Sivak et al. and Google Quantum AI.
milestones.threshold_quote: whose quantum coherence is substantially longer than that of all the imperfect quantum components involved in the QEC process

milestones.title: Increasing a quantum code’s distance reduces its logical error per correction cycle.
milestones.criterion: Within a code family at comparable noise and cycle conditions, increasing code distance—the minimum weight of an undetectable logical error—reduces logical error per cycle. For surface codes, Λ = ε(d)/ε(d+2) must exceed 1. Google, published on 9 December 2024: distances 3, 5 and 7; Λ = 2.14 ± 0.02; 100,000 repetitions per data point. Its 101-qubit distance-7 memory had (0.143 ± 0.003)% error per cycle. Neutral atoms, published on 10 November 2025: distance 3 to 5 gave Λ = 2.14 ± 0.13 over four rounds, without postselection.
milestones.set_by: The quantum-error-correction community’s below-threshold convention; the quoted test uses surface codes.
milestones.threshold_quote: the logical error rate should be suppressed exponentially as we increase the number of physical qubits per logical qubit.

milestones.title: An encoded quantum processor implements a universal set of fault-tolerant logical gates.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate logical gates sufficient to approximate arbitrary quantum circuits while controlling fault propagation. Final error detection and postselection are permitted in the cited implementation. Butt and colleagues, published on 26 January 2026, demonstrated three logical qubits in an eight-qubit trapped-ion code and a universal gate set. Their eight-item, two-solution Grover search used 37,500 shots per measurement basis and achieved single-shot success probability 0.40 ± 0.04, below their optimal classical comparison of 0.46.
milestones.set_by: The field’s universal fault-tolerant gate-set convention; Butt et al.’s quoted implementation uses trapped ions and an error-detecting code.
milestones.threshold_quote: a fault-tolerant universal gate set on an eight-qubit error-detecting code hosting three logical qubits

milestones.title: DOE validates a quantum-computer prototype running a scientific subroutine.
milestones.criterion: DOE verifies an operating prototype’s hardware, software and scientific subroutine. Table 1 illustrates 10 logical qubits and 1,000 hard operations; platform-specific acceptance metrics and evaluation methods are negotiated with DOE.
milestones.set_by: U.S. Department of Energy, Quantum Genesis Q Competition, sections V–VI; metrics are negotiated.
milestones.threshold_quote: validate basic modules in both hardware and software

milestones.title: DOE validates a fault-tolerant quantum computer running a complete scientific workflow.
milestones.criterion: DOE validates a first-generation machine executing a complete scientific workflow, with at least 100 logical qubits and thousands of hard fault-tolerant operations. Table 1 illustrates 100,000 hard operations; metrics are negotiated, and classical intractability is not required. QBI’s roster dated 8 October 2026 lists Stage C developers for all five platforms; stage entry does not establish a DOE workflow-validation pass.
milestones.set_by: U.S. Department of Energy, Quantum Genesis Q Competition, sections V–VI; metrics are negotiated.
milestones.threshold_quote: a full demonstration of a scientific workflow

not_found: No public operating fault-tolerant computer meeting DARPA’s value-greater-than-cost definition was found.
No public DOE validation of a prototype or first-generation scientific workflow was found for any of the five platforms.
Performer-specific DOE acceptance protocols and a common QBI workload, accuracy target and monetary cost model were not found.
